answers.question: What is the product and how big is the trial?
answers.answer: Self-serve invoicing app for freelancers. About 2,400 trial sign-ups a month, 14-day trial, no card required.

answers.question: What is the conversion now and where does it come from?
answers.answer: About 4% trial-to-paid, from our admin dashboard. I have not checked how it is counted.

answers.question: Which tools can your AI reach, and how?
answers.answer: PostHog for product analytics (read), Customer.io for emails (draft access), Stripe read-only.

answers.question: What is the goal and by when?
answers.answer: 7% trial-to-paid by the end of next quarter, without hurting sign-up volume by more than 10%.

answers.question: What may we change?
answers.answer: Onboarding, emails, the paywall and trial length.

answers.question: Where should data live, and who decides?

research.approach: Practitioners first pin down how trial-to-paid is counted, then compare where trial users stall, and find the early product action that separates payers from non-payers. They fix the path to that action first, then add behaviour-triggered and trial-end emails and a clearer paywall, and treat trial length and card requirements as structural tests. Each change runs against a comparison group, with sign-up volume watched so a gain in conversion is not bought with fewer sign-ups.

sources.title: The Conversion Report (ChartMogul)
sources.note: Trials that require a card convert far better than those that do not; time to the first moment of value and clear trial-end terms matter.

sources.title: How to improve free-to-paid conversion (Growth Unhinged)
sources.note: Levers: better-fit sign-ups, faster time to value, plan limits and feature gates, and the pricing page, with one owner for activation tests.

sources.title: Trial expiration reminders (Customer.io docs)
sources.note: Store the trial end date, remind at 7 days and 1 day before expiry, send a trial-ended notice, and count an upgrade within a week of any message.

steps.name: Fix the definition of trial-to-paid and rebuild it from records
steps.why: A dashboard rate can hide a wrong denominator or window. Count sign-ups in a cohort, then payments from Stripe within a stated time after the trial.

steps.name: Collect sign-ups, product events and payments into one table
steps.why: Each trial user needs sign-up date, source, early actions and first payment on one row.

steps.name: Find where trials stall and what payers do first
steps.why: Compare payers with non-payers step by step to find the activation action and the biggest drop-off, and see how long payers take to pay.

steps.name: Review the current onboarding, emails and paywall
steps.why: See which messages and screens a trial user meets, when, and whether trial-end terms are clear.

steps.name: Shorten the path to first value and add behaviour-based and trial-end emails
steps.why: Time to value and timely reminders are the main levers a team without a card requirement controls.

steps.name: Test the paywall, limits and trial length
steps.why: Plan limits and gates move conversion more than small price changes. Trial length and card requirements trade conversion against sign-ups.

steps.name: Read each test against a comparison group and the sign-up limit
steps.why: A trial needs time to finish, and conversion must be read with sign-up volume so a gain is not just fewer, better-fit sign-ups the owner did not want.

pitfalls.text: Quoting a benchmark from a trial type that differs from yours; opt-in trials with no card convert far below card-required trials, so compare like with like.
Reading conversion before the trial and the pay window have closed, so recent cohorts look worse than they are.
Adding a card requirement or shortening the trial to lift conversion while sign-ups fall, ending below the owner's volume limit.
Counting an upgrade as caused by an email when it would have happened anyway; without a comparison group the effect is not known.

stages.name: Review the trial experience today

outputs.name: Email drafts with timing and rules

checks.name: Every launched test is closed with a verdict

hypotheses.statement: The 4% is a counting artifact: the base or window on the dashboard differs from sign-ups and payments in the records.
hypotheses.test: Rebuild the rate from sign-up and Stripe records for closed cohorts and compare with the dashboard.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The rebuilt rate differs from 4% by a clear margin, or test or duplicate sign-ups sit in the base.
hypotheses.refute_if: The rebuilt rate is close to 4% on a clean base.

hypotheses.statement: Most trial users never do the early action that leads to paying.
hypotheses.test: Compare early actions and counts of payers and non-payers in PostHog.
hypotheses.confirm_if: One early action separates payers from non-payers and most trial users never do it.
hypotheses.refute_if: Most trial users do it and still do not pay, or no action separates the groups.

hypotheses.statement: Payers need longer, or shorter, than 14 days, so the trial ends at the wrong moment.
hypotheses.test: Distribution of days from sign-up to first payment, and when non-payers last were active.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Many payers pay near or after day 14, or most non-payers stop using the product long before it.
hypotheses.refute_if: Payment and last use are spread evenly through the trial.

hypotheses.statement: Users who are active hit the paywall or trial end and leave because the value or the next step is unclear.
hypotheses.test: Active users near trial end who do not pay, against the paywall screen and trial-end messages.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A large share of active trial users reach the paywall or trial end and do not pay.
hypotheses.refute_if: Non-payers were mostly inactive well before the paywall.

hypotheses.statement: Trial emails are missing, mistimed or not tied to behaviour.
hypotheses.test: Review current Customer.io campaigns against the trial timeline and what each user did.
hypotheses.confirm_if: No trial-end reminders, or messages do not respond to whether the user took the early action.
hypotheses.refute_if: Timely behaviour-based emails already exist and open and click rates are healthy.

hypotheses.statement: Some sign-up sources bring people unlikely to pay and pull the rate down.
hypotheses.test: Conversion by sign-up source for closed cohorts.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Large sources convert far below the rest.

measurement.window: Read each test on trial cohorts whose 14-day trial and pay window have both closed; expect at least a month per change.
measurement.min_volume: Sign-ups per group as set by the test plan from the 4% baseline; at about 2,400 sign-ups a month, groups of a few hundred read only large effects.
measurement.stop_rule: Stop a change early if monthly sign-ups fall toward the floor of about 2,160, or trial users report a clear problem; otherwise run the full window.
